newsitem.title: USA: North Sea crudes still scarce on U.S. Gulf Coast.
newsitem.headline: North Sea crudes still scarce on U.S. Gulf Coast.

text.p: North Sea crudes remained scarce on the U.S. Gulf Coast on Thursday although several companies were still trying to elicit interest, trade sources said.
The spread between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent was around $1.55-65 a barrel, a level that has prompted a growing list of companies to tentatively offer cargoes into the Gulf Coast.
One top trading house was still trying to work a VLCC, although buyer interest was limited, with many refiners covered through most of March.
One company trying to sell Brent into the Gulf Coast is asking around April WTI minus 20-30 cents a barrel for first-half April arrival.
Meanwhile, the latest cargo of Iraqi crude offered into the U.S. Gulf Coast under the U.N. oil-for-food accord failed to attract buyer interest, traders said.
Cargo-holder Bayoil postponed a possible U.S. arrival date from first-half March into April for Basrah Light in a bid to spark interest in an oversupplied sour market.
Bayoil may be forced to sell the crude elsewhere, sources said.
Traders noted that the March offering was at WTI/Cushing minus $1.70 a barrel. Bayoil is now asking a $2.00 discount to WTI/Cushing for the April cargo, traders said.

Bearish fundamentals for landing sour barrels into the U.S. Gulf led the United Nations to approve an Iraq State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) request to offer special discounts on Basrah Light to U.S. customers.
Basrah Light to the U.S. will drop to a $4.30 discount from a previously agreed $3.85 discount to WTI/Cushing for February to March 9, the last day of the first tranche of the oil-for-food deal.
From March 10, the Basrah Light price will drop to $3.90 under the benchmark.
In Latin America, Chile's state-owned oil company Empresa Nacional del Petroleo (ENAP) bought around 960,000 barrels of Qua Iboe crude from a U.S. company for delivery April 8-12.

Elsewhere, Colombia's state-owned Ecopetrol sold a cargo of Cano Limon loading March 10-13 to a trader at an undisclosed price. The cargo is believed to have been surplus material stemming from Colombia's recently resolved public-sector strike, which cut processing at some Colombian refineries and suppressed local demand, traders said.
The trading house was heard to be reselling the cargo.
An equity producer was also offering two cargoes of Cano Limon loading March 6-8 and March 25-27, asking around April WTI minus $2.00 a barrel.
